lesson.title: Prompts that fit your class
lesson.subtitle: Role, task, context, format, and follow-ups

video.title: Prompts that fit your class
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Amina Bello — primary teacher, Nigeria (main character)
Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

chapters.label: A lesson for the wrong school

scenes.visual: Amina in her crowded Primary 4 classroom, phone in hand. On the phone, a neat lesson plan with a projector, worksheets for everyone and thirty pupils. Behind her: sixty-two pupils, one textbook on her desk, and a ceiling fan that has stopped.
scenes.animation: The plan scrolls up on the phone; the camera pulls back to show the full, busy classroom.
scenes.narration: The chatbot planned my fractions lesson for the wrong school! It assumed a projector, worksheets for everyone and thirty pupils. I have sixty-two pupils, one textbook, and no power after noon.

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card. The Darsi mark pops in, then the course name, the lesson title and a yellow ‘AI’ track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark scales 0→100% with a small overshoot (≤ 200 ms); title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: prompts that fit your class.

scenes.visual: The chatbot as a simple box with a blindfold-like band: it cannot see Amina’s classroom. A thought bubble shows a generic, average classroom that matches no real one.
scenes.animation: The classroom details (pupils, textbook, fan) fade in behind the box, unseen by it; the generic classroom pops up in its bubble.
scenes.narration: The chatbot wasn’t careless. It knows nothing about your class: your pupils’ age, how many, what you have, the language they think in. So it predicts the most typical answer: an average classroom, which is nobody’s.

scenes.visual: A prompt builds on a card, one coloured ingredient at a time: role, task, context, format, each with its own label.
scenes.animation: Each ingredient slides in and snaps onto the card as it is said (≤ 300 ms).
scenes.narration: A strong prompt has four ingredients. A role: “You’re a primary maths teacher in Nigeria.” A task: “Plan a forty-minute lesson on halves and quarters.” Context: “Primary Four, sixty-two pupils, one textbook, no projector, Hausa at home.” And a format: “Numbered steps with timings, and one exit question.”

scenes.visual: Amina pastes one of her own word problems into the prompt: Musa sharing mangoes with friends. The chatbot returns five new problems in the same style.
scenes.animation: The example card drops into the prompt; five similar cards fan out of the reply.
scenes.narration: When you want a certain style, show one. “Here’s a word problem my pupils loved: Musa shares twelve mangoes with three friends. Write five more like it.” One good example often says more than a paragraph of instructions.

scenes.visual: Clean white card with the AI track chip: ‘Prompt’ at the top, and three cards for what only the teacher knows: the pupils, the room, the resources.
scenes.animation: The three cards pop in one by one (300 ms apart).
scenes.narration: So, a prompt is what you tell an AI tool to do. Its most important part is often the context: what only you know about your pupils, room and resources. That makes the answer fit.

scenes.visual: Amina hands a note to a relief teacher at the classroom door. The note grows from “Teach fractions” to a full list: Primary 4, 62 pupils, one textbook, start with halves, power goes at noon.
scenes.animation: Lines are added to the note one by one; the relief teacher nods.
scenes.narration: It’s like briefing a relief teacher who has never seen your school. “Teach fractions” isn’t enough. You’d say: Primary Four, sixty-two pupils, one textbook, start with halves, and the power goes at noon.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma pops in holding a phone with a one-line prompt: “Write ten maths questions.” Three answer cards drop in below her.
scenes.animation: Character slides in from the side; answer cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Amina’s prompt says: “Write ten maths questions.” What would help most?

scenes.visual: The card ‘Her pupils’ age, level and resources’ gets a check badge. Split screen: without context, a generic answer; with context, an answer that names Primary 4, sixty-two pupils and Kano.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops (150 ms); the two columns fill as they are said.
scenes.narration: Her pupils’ age, level and resources. Being polite doesn’t hurt, and “excellent” sounds good, but neither says anything about Primary Four in Kano. Context turns a typical answer into one that fits.

scenes.visual: A chat on Amina’s phone: her short follow-up messages appear one after another, and the plan on screen changes after each one.
scenes.animation: Each follow-up bubble slides up; the plan above it shrinks, gains local names, gains a harder version.
scenes.narration: When the first answer isn’t right, don’t start again. Follow up, as with a colleague. “Make it shorter.” “Use names and foods from Kano.” “Add a harder version for fast finishers.” And “Now in Hausa”, then check it with someone who speaks Hausa.

scenes.visual: A phone screen with the lab: ingredient buttons (Role, Task, Context, Format, Language), the prompt they build, a prompt-strength bar and an ‘Ask the AI’ button with the example answer under it.
scenes.animation: Buttons light up one by one; the strength bar fills; the example answer changes after each tap.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: build a better prompt
scenes.narration: In the app, build a prompt from ingredients. A role and a task are already on. Add the context, a format and the language, ask the AI each time, and watch its water-cycle questions get more useful.

scenes.visual: Amina holds up a long lesson plan that spills off her phone, next to a clock showing 40 minutes. Three answer cards appear beside her.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. The plan is good, but far too long for my forty minutes. What should I do?

scenes.visual: The follow-up card gets the check badge, then the screen resolves into four summary lines and an orange takeaway bar.
scenes.animation: Lines tick in 250 ms apart; the takeaway bar slides up.
scenes.narration: Follow up, and ask it to fit forty minutes. Remember: the AI can’t see your class. Give it a role, a task, context and a format, and an example when style matters. Then follow up until it fits.

scenes.visual: Amina’s classroom: a weak prompt and its vague answer on the board. Groups each hold up one ingredient card and call out how the answer will change.
scenes.animation: Ingredient cards rise from each group; arrows point to the changes on the board.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: a prompt makeover. Show a weak prompt and the answer it got. Each group adds one ingredient, a role, the context or a format, and predicts how the answer will change. If you have a phone, test one together.

checkpoints.prompt: Amina’s prompt says: “Write ten maths questions.” What would help most?

options.text: Her pupils’ age, level and resources

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — the AI can’t see her class. Age, level and resources are the context that makes the questions fit.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — politeness and big words tell the AI nothing about her class. Context does: age, level and resources.

checkpoints.prompt: The plan is good, but too long for 40 minutes. What should Amina do?

options.text: Start again in a new chat
Use it and rush the end

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a follow-up keeps what was good and fixes what wasn’t.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — starting again throws away what was good, and rushing hurts the lesson. Follow up: ask it to fit 40 minutes.
